lessons.title: Introduction to Belt Grinders and Abrasives
lessons.body: A belt grinder is the workhorse of any bladesmithing shop. In Africa, you can build a simple 2x72-inch belt grinder using a 1.5 kW (2 HP) electric motor, a set of wheels, and a steel frame. Many makers in Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa start with a locally fabricated grinder to keep costs down. The most common belt size is 2x72 inches (50x1830 mm), but 2x48 or 4x36 also work. Belts come in different abrasives: aluminium oxide for wood and mild steel, zirconia for heavy grinding on hardened steel, and ceramic for fast cutting and long life. Grit sizes range from 24 (very coarse) to 2000 (very fine). Start with 36 or 50 grit for profiling, then move to 120, 220, 400, and up to 800 for finishing. Always grind with the belt moving away from the edge to avoid overheating and ruining the temper. Use a speed of around 1500-3000 surface feet per minute (SFM) for steel. For a 2x72 belt, that means a motor RPM of about 1750 with a 4-inch drive wheel. Keep a container of water nearby to cool the blade; dip frequently. Safety first: wear eye protection, a dust mask, and never wear loose clothing. In many African workshops, you'll find grinders made from repurposed car alternators or washing machine motors, but a dedicated motor is better. Learn to change belts quickly and track them properly. A well-tuned grinder with sharp belts will save you hours of hand sanding.

lessons.title: Grinding Bevels: Flat, Saber, and Hollow
lessons.body: Bevels are the ground angles that form the cutting edge. There are three main types: flat, saber, and hollow. Flat grinds are the easiest for beginners. You grind the entire side of the blade at a consistent angle, usually 2-5 degrees per side, until you reach the desired edge thickness. For a chef's knife, aim for a bevel height of about 15-20 mm and an edge thickness of 0.5 mm before sharpening. Saber grinds have a flat bevel that doesn't go all the way to the spine; the top part of the blade remains flat. This is common on bushcraft knives. To grind a saber bevel, mark a line on the blade where the bevel should stop, then grind up to that line. Hollow grinds are made with a contact wheel, usually 6 to 10 inches in diameter. The wheel creates a concave curve. Hollow grinds are popular on hunting knives and straight razors. Use a wheel that matches your desired curve. For all grinds, the key is consistency: keep the blade moving, use light pressure, and let the belt do the work. In Africa, many smiths use a simple jig made from angle iron to hold the blade at a constant angle. You can also grind freehand, but practice on scrap steel first. After grinding, check for symmetry by looking at the blade from the top and bottom. The bevels should be even. If one side is wider, grind a little more on that side. Always grind with the edge facing away from the belt rotation to avoid catching. Cool the blade often in water to prevent overheating. A good grind sets the foundation for a sharp, durable edge.

lessons.title: Achieving Symmetry and Clean Plunge Lines
lessons.body: Symmetry is what separates a professional-looking blade from a homemade one. Plunge lines are the vertical transitions where the bevel meets the ricasso (the flat part above the handle). Clean plunge lines are sharp and even on both sides. To achieve this, first ensure your blade is flat and parallel. Use a file guide or a grinding jig to set your angle. Many African bladesmiths make a simple jig from a piece of hardwood and a bolt. Clamp the blade in the jig, set the angle, and grind one side. Then flip the blade and grind the other side using the same jig setting. This ensures the bevels match. For plunge lines, use a file guide clamped to the ricasso. This acts as a hard stop for the belt. Grind slowly and check often. A common mistake is to grind too much on one side. Use a marker to color the bevel; as you grind, the marker disappears, showing you where you've cut. When you're close to the final shape, switch to a finer belt (e.g., 220 grit) and use light pressure. For the plunge line, you can also use a round file to refine the transition. After grinding, inspect the blade under good light. Look for any uneven spots. If one bevel is wider, grind a little more on that side. Remember, it's easier to remove more steel than to put it back. So go slow. Once you have symmetry, you can move to hand sanding. A well-ground blade with clean plunge lines will need less sanding and will look much better. Practice on mild steel until you can consistently produce symmetrical bevels.

lessons.title: Hand Sanding and Polishing Techniques
lessons.body: Hand sanding is the most time-consuming part of bladesmithing, but it's what gives a blade its final look. After grinding, start with a 120-grit sandpaper to remove deep scratches. Then move to 220, 400, 600, 800, and up to 2000 for a mirror polish. Always sand in one direction, then change direction 90 degrees when you switch grits. This helps you see when you've removed the previous scratches. Use a sanding block or a piece of hardwood with sandpaper wrapped around it. For African makers, locally available sandpaper from hardware stores works fine. Waterproof paper is best because you can use it with water or oil to reduce clogging. For a satin finish, stop at 400 or 600 grit and sand in one direction. For a mirror finish, continue to 2000 grit and then use a buffing wheel with white compound. When sanding, keep the blade flat on the block to avoid rounding the edges. If you're sanding a bevel, use a backing block that matches the angle. Many smiths use a piece of glass or a granite tile as a backing surface. For the handle, sand to at least 400 grit for a smooth feel. If you're working with wood, raise the grain with a damp cloth between grits. For a polished blade, after sanding, clean it with acetone or alcohol to remove any oil. Then apply a thin coat of oil or wax to protect it from rust. In humid African climates, rust is a constant enemy, so a protective finish is essential. Remember, patience is key. Rushing hand sanding will show in the final product.

lessons.title: Etching and Finishing for Pattern-Welded Steel
lessons.body: Pattern-welded steel, such as Damascus, shows its beauty through etching. After grinding and sanding to at least 600 grit, clean the blade thoroughly with acetone or dish soap to remove all oil and dirt. Then mix a solution of ferric chloride and water. In Africa, ferric chloride can be found at electronics supply shops or made by dissolving iron in hydrochloric acid (careful!). A common ratio is 1 part ferric chloride to 3 parts water. For a stronger etch, use 1:1. Wear gloves and eye protection. Dip the blade in the solution for 5-10 minutes. The acid eats the softer steel faster, revealing the pattern. Check every minute. When the pattern is deep enough, remove the blade and rinse with water, then neutralize with baking soda solution. For a contrast, you can lightly sand the blade with 2000 grit to remove the black oxides from the raised areas, leaving the darker etched areas. This is called

the pattern. For a final finish, apply a coat of oil or wax. Some smiths use a coffee etch to darken the steel further. To do this, soak the blade in strong black coffee for 24 hours. This works well on carbon steel Damascus. After etching, the blade is susceptible to rust, so oil it immediately. In Africa, where humidity is high, consider using a protective lacquer or a thin layer of beeswax. Always work in a well-ventilated area when etching. Dispose of the acid properly; never pour it down the drain. With practice, you can achieve stunning patterns that make your knives stand out.

lessons.title: Sharpening and Honing the Edge
lessons.body: Sharpening is the final step. A sharp knife is safe and effective. Start by establishing a bevel angle. For most knives, 15-20 degrees per side is good. Use a sharpening stone or a belt grinder with a fine belt (e.g., 400-800 grit). If using stones, soak a water stone for 10 minutes. Place the blade on the stone at the desired angle. Use a marker on the edge to check your angle. Push the blade across the stone as if slicing a thin layer off the top. Do 10 strokes on one side, then 10 on the other. Repeat until you feel a burr on the opposite side of the edge. A burr is a tiny lip of metal that you can feel with your finger. Once you have a burr along the entire edge, switch to a finer stone (1000-3000 grit) and repeat, but with lighter pressure. Then use a leather strop with polishing compound to remove the burr and polish the edge. In Africa, you can make a strop from a piece of leather glued to a wooden board. Use green or white compound. Strop 20 times per side. Test sharpness by slicing paper or shaving arm hair. If it doesn't cut, repeat. For a convex edge, use a slack belt on your grinder. Always maintain a consistent angle. A simple trick is to use a coin under the spine to set the angle. For field sharpening, carry a small diamond stone. Remember, a sharp knife requires less force and is safer. After sharpening, clean the blade and apply a thin coat of oil. Store your knife in a dry place. With practice, you can get a razor-sharp edge every time.

quiz.q: What is the most common belt size for a bladesmithing belt grinder?
quiz.explanation: The 2x72-inch belt is the industry standard for knife making due to its versatility and availability.

quiz.q: Which abrasive is best for grinding hardened steel?
quiz.explanation: Ceramic belts cut faster and last longer on hardened steel, though they are more expensive.

quiz.q: What grit size should you start with for profiling a blade?
quiz.explanation: 36 grit is coarse enough to remove material quickly without being too aggressive.

quiz.q: Why should you grind with the belt moving away from the edge?
options: B) To prevent the blade from catching
C) To get a smoother finish
quiz.explanation: Grinding into the edge can cause the belt to catch and throw the blade, which is dangerous.

quiz.q: What is the recommended surface feet per minute (SFM) for grinding steel?
quiz.explanation: 1500-3000 SFM is the typical range for steel grinding to balance material removal and heat control.

quiz.q: What is a flat grind?
options: A) A bevel that is concave
B) A bevel that goes all the way to the spine
C) A bevel that is flat and usually goes from edge to spine
D) A bevel that is convex
quiz.explanation: A flat grind is a straight bevel from the edge to the spine, common on chef's knives.

quiz.q: What is a saber grind?
options: A) A flat grind that stops before the spine
D) A grind with a secondary bevel
quiz.explanation: A saber grind is a flat bevel that does not reach the spine, leaving a flat section on the upper blade.

quiz.q: What tool is used to create a hollow grind?
quiz.explanation: A contact wheel, typically 6-10 inches in diameter, creates the concave curve of a hollow grind.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a file guide when grinding?
options: B) To set a consistent angle
D) To measure the blade length
quiz.explanation: A file guide clamps to the blade and provides a hard stop to maintain a consistent bevel angle.

quiz.q: How can you check for symmetry after grinding bevels?
options: B) Look from the top and bottom
quiz.explanation: Viewing the blade from the top and bottom reveals if the bevels are even on both sides.

quiz.q: What is a plunge line?
options: A) The edge of the blade
B) The transition where the bevel meets the ricasso
C) The spine of the blade
D) The tip of the blade
quiz.explanation: The plunge line is the vertical line where the bevel grinding stops and the ricasso begins.

quiz.q: Why is it important to use a marker when grinding bevels?
options: B) To see where you've ground
quiz.explanation: Marking the bevel shows your progress as the marker is removed by grinding.

quiz.q: What grit sandpaper should you start with after grinding?
quiz.explanation: 120 grit removes the scratches left by the grinder without taking too long.

quiz.q: Why should you change sanding direction between grits?
options: B) To see when previous scratches are removed
quiz.explanation: Changing direction 90 degrees makes it easier to see if you've removed all scratches from the previous grit.

quiz.q: What is the highest grit typically used for a mirror polish?
quiz.explanation: 2000 grit is often the final step before buffing for a mirror finish.

quiz.q: What is a satin finish?
options: B) A finish with visible scratches in one direction
quiz.explanation: A satin finish has fine, uniform scratches in one direction, usually achieved by stopping at 400-600 grit.

quiz.q: What should you use to protect a blade from rust in humid climates?
quiz.explanation: A thin coat of oil or wax creates a barrier against moisture, preventing rust.

quiz.q: What chemical is commonly used to etch pattern-welded steel?
quiz.explanation: Ferric chloride is the most common etchant for Damascus steel, revealing the pattern.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of neutralizing after etching?
options: A) To stop the acid from eating further
quiz.explanation: Neutralizing with baking soda stops the acid reaction and prevents over-etching.

quiz.q: What is a coffee etch used for?
quiz.explanation: A coffee etch darkens the steel, especially the softer areas, enhancing contrast in Damascus.

quiz.q: What is the recommended angle for sharpening most knives?
quiz.explanation: 15-20 degrees per side is a good compromise between sharpness and edge retention for most knives.

quiz.q: What is a burr?
options: A) A type of sharpening stone
B) A tiny lip of metal on the edge
quiz.explanation: A burr is a raised lip of metal that forms on the opposite side of the edge when sharpening.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a leather strop?
options: A) To remove the burr and polish the edge
quiz.explanation: Stropping on leather with compound removes the burr and polishes the edge to a razor finish.

quiz.q: How can you set a consistent sharpening angle without a jig?
options: A) Use a coin under the spine
quiz.explanation: A coin under the spine raises the blade to a consistent angle, a common field trick.

quiz.q: What is a convex edge?
options: C) A bevel with a rounded profile
quiz.explanation: A convex edge is rounded, often achieved by grinding on a slack belt, and is strong for chopping.

quiz.q: Why is a sharp knife safer than a dull one?
options: B) It requires less force and is less likely to slip
quiz.explanation: A sharp knife cuts with less pressure, reducing the chance of slipping and cutting yourself.

quiz.q: What is the best way to clean a blade before etching?
quiz.explanation: Acetone or alcohol removes all oils and dirt, ensuring an even etch.

quiz.q: What safety gear should you wear when grinding?
options: B) Eye protection and dust mask
quiz.explanation: Eye protection, dust mask, earplugs, and a leather apron are all recommended for grinding safety.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a slack belt on a grinder?
quiz.explanation: A slack belt (no backing) allows the belt to conform to the blade, creating a convex edge.

quiz.q: How often should you dip the blade in water while grinding?
options: C) Frequently, whenever it gets hot
quiz.explanation: Dip frequently to keep the blade cool and prevent overheating, which can ruin the temper.
